sections.html:
• Common name: Mermaid Weed
  • Other names: Marsh mermaidweed
  • Scientific name: Proserpinaca palustris
  • Difficulty: Medium
  • Lighting: Moderate-High
  • Optimal pH: 5.5 – 7.5
  • Optimal GH: 2 – 8
  • Optimal temperature: 15 – 30°C (59 – 86°F)
  • Substrate: Nutrient-rich
  • Can be grown emersed: Yes
  • Growth rate: Slow to moderate
  • Placement in tank: Midground and background
  • Aquarium size: over 50 cm (20+ inches)
  • Fertilizers needed: CO2
  • Propagation: Vegetative, by cuttings
  • Color: Red, yellow, orange, and green

Proserpinaca palustris is found across various regions in North America, including the United States and Canada.

In the United States, it is distributed in states such as Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

Additionally, it can be found in Canadian provinces like New Brunswick, Ontario, and Quebec, as well as in countries such as Jamaica, Cuba, the Bahamas, Mexico (specifically in the states of Chiapas and Veracruz-Llave), Guatemala, El Salvador, and Colombia.

Proserpinaca palustris is a freshwater plant. It generally grows in shallow swamps, ponds, or temporary pools.

This plant tolerates a submerged condition remarkably well but also needs air-breathing intervals for its life cycle.
The recommended tank size for growing Mermaid Weed is a minimum of about 40 litres (10 gallons). Because of its growth potential, tall tanks are better than long tanks for this plant.

• In aquariums, this plant is commonly used as a classic stem plant, planted in dense groups along the sides and as a mid or background plant due to its larger size.
  • Depending on the conditions, this plant has a slow to moderate growth rate. For example, you will get 1-2 inches in a month with poor lighting and no CO2.
  • Underwater, it shows its best decorative qualities. Do not allow it to grow above the surface. Start trimming when there are 10-15 cm (4-6 inches) left to the water surface.
  • Under optimal conditions, it does not grow ugly aerial roots.

Fertilization: Proper and regular fertilization, as well as the right concentration of CO2, is crucial. A deficiency in iron and/or potassium results in overall discoloration and leaf loss. This plant is not demanding of phosphates but reacts negatively to an excess of nitrates.

It is recommended to dose liquid plant fertilizers regularly (2-3 times a week) and root tabs periodically.

Planting: Plant it deep enough in the substrate to keep it from floating up. Unlike some plants that can be left floating until their root system develops, it is not advisable to do so with Proserpinaca palustris.

Temperature: Mermaid Weed will thrive in a broad temperature range from 15 – 30°C (60 – 86°F), making it suitable for cold-water aquariums. At high temperatures above 28°C (82°F), the internodes become long regardless of the amount of light. At 18 – 25°C (64 – 77°F), the plant looks much more decorative.

pH: This plant prefers a pH in the range of 5.5 – 7.5. Hardness: It grows better in soft and medium water, GH 2 – 8 and KH 1 – 4.

Flow: In nature, Mermaid Weed grows in stagnant waters. It does not like strong flow very much.

Lighting: The lighting should be strong as Mermaid Weed loves light and dies in the shade.

Under good lighting, the leaves acquire a beautiful red-copper color, making the plant a pleasant contrast with other plants. In low lighting, it has green leaves and an unattractive thick stem, about twice as thick as under optimal conditions.

According to one study, it tends to grow juvenile (undeveloped) leaves with an 8-hour light cycle, generative (mature) leaves with a 12-hour light cycle, and generative leaves and flowers with a 14-hour light cycle.

If light does not reach the lower part of the stem, it drops the lower leaves. The plant also tends to drop its lower leaves when the upper stem reaches the surface.

Substrate: This plant is a heavy root feeder. If the substrate is inadequate, the stem blackens and the plant deteriorates. A nutrient-rich substrate is therefore ideal. The substrate depth should be at least 5 cm (2 inches) since the root system is well-developed. It does not tolerate root trimming well.

CO2: Although some aquarists have managed to grow Mermaid Weed without CO2, it is more of an exception. Without CO2, you will not achieve the bright red-yellow coloration that this plant is known for. However, high CO2 concentrations can also cause morphological mutations in the leaves, making them thinner with elongated teeth.

In its emersed forms, Proserpinaca palustris reproduces through seeds, which is most suitable for outdoor cultivation.

In aquariums (submersed form), it can be propagated from stem cuttings.

  • Take a healthy stem cutting, making sure it has several leaves and nodes.
  • Cut it between the nodes.
  • Remove any leaves from the lower portion of the cutting and plant it in the substrate.

Propagation is lackluster. It only produces side shoots when trimmed, and even then usually only 1 to 3 at a time. Those side shoots also grow very slowly.

Melting: there are many reasons why this plant can melt all of a sudden.

  • Transition from an emersed form to a submersed form.
  • Sudden changes in water parameters.
  • Too hard and/or alkaline pH.
  • Low lighting, overshadowing, and short photoperiod.
  • Not enough fertilization and CO2.

Discoloration: depending on environmental conditions, the plant can display colors from light green to red and even purple. Achieving a red hue is often impossible without optimal conditions. In low-tech aquariums (no CO2, low light), the primary color will be green with a slight yellowish tint.

Leggy bottom: when Mermaid Weed gets really large (or reaches the surface), the lower leaves may die back, leaving a bare, elongated lower stem. Top leaves start blocking the light for the lower leaves. Solution: prune the plant, check the lighting and provide CO2.

Relocation: the plant may melt after relocation or propagation by splitting, even within the same tank. It does not like to be disturbed, and cutting roots will negatively affect it.

Nutrient sensitive: this plant cannot survive without nutrition for a long time. Solution: regular feeding.

Algae: due to its relatively slow growth, the plant is more susceptible to being covered in algae.

Benefits: the color, shape, and form make it an excellent decorative addition to any aquascape. It produces small pearls of oxygen on top of the plant. Its well-developed root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate. It serves as cover and a hiding place for invertebrates and small fish, and acts as a buffet of biofilm for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Conclusion: to achieve its desired classic look, this plant requires CO2, nutrient-rich substrate, regular fertilization, and strong lighting, all perfectly balanced. It will struggle in a low-tech tank, so it is more suitable for experienced aquarists.

If you keep shrimp with Mermaid Weed: a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.
